sentences.text: The defining feature of this animal is a single, elongated tooth roughly one centimetre in length.
Edward Drinker Cope first misidentified the holotype specimen as belonging to a marine reptile before correcting his assessment to a carnivorous dinosaur within the same year.
A related species, Paronychodon caperatus, has been found in rock layers from North Dakota, Montana, South Dakota, and Wyoming.
The type specimen for this second species is a tooth similar in form but somewhat larger than the original.
Scientists have debated whether this animal was a coelurid, ornithomimosaur, dromaeosaurid, archaeopterygid, or troodontid, though it may simply be another type of coelurosaurian theropod.
Current tentative classifications place the family within Troodontidae.
These creatures inhabited North America at the very end of the Cretaceous period, approximately 70 million years ago.
The fossil record for this group spans a vast interval from 154.8 million years ago down to 66 million years ago.
While most researchers view these teeth as belonging to indeterminate theropods, a small consensus suggests they belong to Deinonychosauria.
No adult jaws bearing identical teeth have ever been discovered.
One early theory proposed by Othniel Charles Marsh suggested the teeth were pathological, formed when lower jaw teeth accidentally grew back-to-back on the mandible suture.
